issues.legal_issue: An executing court may examine a decree’s validity only when the objection is that the court which passed it lacked inherent jurisdiction, and may decline to enforce the decree if that defect renders it a nullity.
material_facts: The decree-holder sought to execute an ex-parte decree for possession.
The judgment-debtor objected to execution, arguing that the civil court lacked jurisdiction because the land was governed by the land reforms law.
The executing court found that the land had ceased to be agricultural land, and the Supreme Court held that the decree was not a nullity.
issues.conclusion: An executing court may consider an objection based on inherent lack of jurisdiction, but the objection in this case failed because no such lack of jurisdiction was established.
issues.legal_principle: An executing court generally cannot go behind a decree or question its legality or correctness, but it may refuse execution if the decree is a nullity for want of the passing court’s inherent jurisdiction. The Court relied on Hira Lal Patni v Sri Kali Nath, Sunder Dass v Ram Prakash, Kiran Singh v Chaman Paswan, and Gaon Sabha v Nathi.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party is seeking to enforce a court decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.decree_challenged_for_inherent_jurisdict: The objector argues that the court that passed the decree lacked inherent jurisdiction over the subject matter or parties.
predicates.inherent_jurisdiction_absent: The court that passed the decree lacked inherent jurisdiction, making the decree a nullity.

issues.definition: When a decree is being enforced and an objector establishes that the court that passed it lacked inherent jurisdiction, the executing court may decline enforcement.

issues.legal_issue: Land that has ceased to be used for purposes connected with agriculture and has been built upon or converted into plots is not agricultural land governed by the land reforms law, so the statutory bar on civil-court jurisdiction does not apply to a civil possession suit concerning it.
material_facts: The decree arose from a civil suit under the summary possession remedy, which did not require determination of title.
The executing court found that the land had ceased to be agricultural and was not being used for purposes contemplated by the land reforms law.
Electricity bills and the urbanized character of the area supported the finding that the land had lost its agricultural character.
The findings that the land was no longer agricultural were not squarely challenged before the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: Because the land had ceased to be agricultural when the suit was instituted, the statutory bar did not apply, the civil court had jurisdiction, and the decree was not a nullity.
issues.legal_principle: The land reforms law’s definition of land covers land held or occupied for purposes connected with agriculture, horticulture, or animal husbandry. Land that is no longer used for those purposes and has been built upon or converted into plots ceases to be agricultural land for that law, so the jurisdictional bar does not apply. The Court relied on Ram Lubbaya Kapoor v J R Chawla, Narain Singh v Financial Commissioner, Neelima Gupta v Yogesh Saroha, and Anand J Datwani v Geeti Bhagat Datwani; it also applied the jurisdictional rule in Hira Lal Patni v Sri Kali Nath.

predicates.civil_possession_suit: A party brings a civil suit seeking possession of land after alleged dispossession.
predicates.land_not_used_for_agricultural_purposes: The land is not being held or occupied for agricultural, horticultural, or animal-husbandry purposes.
predicates.land_built_up_or_converted: The land has been built upon or converted into plots or a developed colony.

issues.definition: A civil court has jurisdiction over a possession suit when the land is no longer used for agricultural purposes and has been built upon or converted.
